title: T1055.014 — Process Injection - VDSO Hijacking
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Process Injection - VDSO Hijacking with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Animated diagram of vDSO hijacking. An attacker gets a shell on a Linux server through an exposed service, uses ptrace to open a resident daemon's memory, reads /proc/2041/maps to find the vDSO page, patches clock_gettime with bootstrap code, the daemon runs the code when it asks for the time, the payload downloads and the original vDSO bytes are restored, the payload beacons out and CPU spikes, and finally defenders isolate the host, compare the vDSO with a clean baseline, and hunt the fleet.

steps.title: Foothold
steps.caption: The attacker reaches a Linux server through an exposed management service and gets a shell as a service account. Nothing unusual is visible yet, because the login looks like normal automation. a new execve by a service account that never logs in interactively is the first weak signal
steps.defender: EDR and Sysmon record the process, memory and image-load events. Correlate them with the parent process.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Write primitive
steps.caption: The attacker picks a daemon that runs for months and will not restart. Using ptrace, the Linux debugging interface, they attach to the process and gain the ability to read and write its memory. auditd records a successful ptrace attach. Long-running daemons are almost never debugged in production
steps.defender: EDR and Sysmon record the process, memory and image-load events. Correlate them with the parent process.

steps.title: Locate the vDSO
steps.caption: The attacker reads /proc/2041/maps . This file lists every memory mapping of the process, including the line marked [vdso] with its exact address range. an unusual process opened another process's memory map. This is rare outside debuggers and performance tools
steps.defender: EDR and Sysmon record the process, memory and image-load events. Correlate them with the parent process.

steps.title: Patch the time function
steps.caption: The attacker writes small bootstrap shellcode over the clock_gettime function inside the [vdso] page. The daemon calls this function many times per second, so the trap will trigger at once. the eBPF sensor fires the critical alert, a memory write landed inside the [vdso] mapping
steps.defender: EDR and Sysmon record the process, memory and image-load events. Correlate them with the parent process.

steps.title: Trigger
steps.caption: The daemon asks for the time. The patched function runs the bootstrap code inside the trusted daemon. No new process or thread was created, so process-list based tools see nothing new. execution from the vDSO region is flagged and pairs with the write alert from the previous step
steps.defender: EDR and Sysmon record the process, memory and image-load events. Correlate them with the parent process.

steps.title: Payload and cleanup
steps.caption: The bootstrap code downloads the real payload, starts it inside or beside the daemon, and then restores the original vDSO bytes. A memory scanner now sees a clean page. This is the self-healing hook. the integrity scanner reports a matching hash. Do not close the case; correlate with the earlier write alert

steps.caption: Defenders isolate the host, hash the vDSO against a clean baseline saved for the same kernel version, harden ptrace settings, and hunt every server for the same pattern. containment and a fleet-wide hunt turn one alert into a full scope check
